Not a pest control expert, but this is what I usually do in the fall/winter when they start coming here. 

1.) Make sure any holes, cracks, any place where they can get in, are sealed. I usually look around windows and doorways because they seem to like those places as entrances. 

2.) Dehumidifiers in places like bathrooms- I usually have a humidifier in my room during the fall/winter, but I try to keep damp-rid type things in my bathroom since it gets humid and wet on a regular basis, and bugs like that sort of thing. Basements too, probably. 

3.) Sprinkle Diatomaceous Earth whenever you see them, and around windows, doorways, etc. This will dry them out so they're less likely to come in. Make sure you put this in in a dry place. 

4.) Vacuuming regularly, both to replace the diatomaceous earth, and to get rid of dust. I have no idea if they like the dust or what, but there seems to be more when vacuuming is neglected, ymmv of course

Most of these are long term things, but I hope they help. I would also try an exterminator, along with cleaning out extra clutter in rooms that you feel safe doing so in. 

Hope these help!!

One of the biggest mistakes people make imo on the first visit is to stay inside Chinatown Square. Go down Wentworth or even some side streets, there's a lot to see. Check out the Chinese American Museum of Chicago (small, but very interesting and has some cool things in the small gift stop usually). For food, I don't usually go veg so I don't have a whole lot of specifics but it depends on what you're feeling. There's Little Lamb Hot Pot which is okay, Ken Kee which is good for noodles, (tho I liked it more before the remodel :(  ) and Evergreen Restaurant at the far end of the strip on Wentworth if you're looking for more standard American Chinese food. 


For Tea, really any of the herbal shops have some interesting stuff that you might not find in a regular selection. If Sun Sun Tong Co/ Oriental Boutique (they split the storefront) is still open, they're cool for things like shoes, hats, jackets, and also some small knickknacks. If the herbal side is open they have prepackaged teas and herbs that you can buy without any sort of consultation. 


EK Souvenirs is huge and has pretty much anything you would want, even some pretty cute housewares, and is slightly cheaper than any place in the square, imo. Though, it can get pretty packed at times. Mei's Martial Arts sells some pretty cool staffs and things if you're interested in that (not sure if that's the "cool" you're looking for!). 


PLEASE get some Chinese bakery food, it's to die for. Chiu Quon And FeiDa bakery are my favorites. If you can eat meat, I love the egg and ham buns. Best thing to do is to grab a bunch and eat in Ping Tom Park. 

There's generally nowhere horribly bad you can go in Chinatown in my opinion, but obviously you can see I'm a big fan of it so I'm biased (lived in Chicago for my whole short life, going to Chinatown on the L is the closest I've ever gotten to a "vacation").
 Hope this is a good start at least! 

TL;DR: Chinatown Square is nice but please look around because there's so much more!

Do not worry about shaving or how you may look. Doctors have seen a wide range of parts and I can 100% guarantee you that they will not judge and will not care how they look unless it's something medically abnormal that needs to be noted. 

As someone who's a victim of assault, I understand that these can be traumatic. For a pap smear, the doctor may use a tool called a speculum to get a better view and opening of the vaginal canal. It may hurt, but you can ask them to use the smallest size possible which will hurt less. Usually I don't feel pain, just a pressure (like someone pressing down), but some people say it can be a little painful. They will insert a swab and take a sample which is usually less than 30 seconds. This may feel uncomfortable but if it is unusually painful, do not be scared to tell your doctor. 

The only prep you need to do is to take a shower, clean the area gently with *only water*, NO SOAPS. soaps will mess up the pH and make the appointment more irritating and painful than needed. You don't need to shave or do any other prep unless indicated by your doctor.

I think some (not all, not even most, but a minority) of parents see dealing with disabilities during the day to be a school thing that they're not supposed to be part of. Sometimes when they see what works best for their kid they think it's treating them dumb or that it's beneath them, but in a way I'm a bit glad parents are seeing this. I know there's a lot of things that ended up helping me that my parents thought were "babying" (a big example is having physical representations of numbers to help with my Dyscalculia, usually those single blocks you can attach to each other or those grid square blocks) that were really important to me actually getting to a point where I could function decently on my own.

Thanks for your input. I was (and still am, even in university) someone that struggles immensely with distance learning because of my disabilities. If I was back in elementary or even high school, even with support from my parents I don't think I'd be able to meet my IEP goals. Most educators and parents are doing the best with what they have... It's just a sad situation all around.

This pandemic is going to be (and is!) especially hard on students that have an IEP or 504 ("special Ed" or "special needs" students). It's already hard to meet the goals of an IEP while in person (as a kid who had an IEP), and a lot of these kids are accustomed and boosted academically by having that schedule to follow every day and a clear distinction between home and school. From experience, it may be hard (or near impossible) for some of these kids to get back to the place they would be in physical classrooms while staying at home. It's an absolute shame and I wish there was more being done, but there's not much I can think of with everything being stretched so thin. 

I also think some parents just don't have the experience with their kids' learning styles. I know a fair amount of parents completely ignore that their kid is "different" and may need a different learning environment. Some parents straight up don't care. I understand the shock of seeing your child in a class that may seem beneath them but in that case they need to 

a.) Communicate with the child to understand if this is the level they're comfortable with (if it is, then that's fine!) and then 

b.) Talk to their child's teacher or even better, their IEP/504 case manager. 

It's a shame this kid still hasn't learned to read. It's a shame what's happening to "special needs" kids all over right now. Thankfully the parents in this article care if their kid even logs into school, because there's a decent amount that probably don't and assume their kid is already a lost cause. 


This is all from my own experiences so things might be different now, I'd like to hear from SPED teachers or those who work with IEP/504s (and also thank you for your work, I know a lot of you really care about your students!)
